Each item below is a decision point in an AI-safety research project. You get the kind of decision, a short statement of the problem the team faced, and the text of their write-up that comes BEFORE the decision. You do not see what they decided, and you must not guess it.

For each item write the decision point as a researcher would have faced it, BEFORE choosing:
- "context": 2-4 sentences, neutral third person ("A research team ..."). The setting, what they were studying, and what they knew at that moment; for a decision about interpreting, accepting or stating a result, the result itself. Give the facts that any reasonable option would need. The excerpt may already announce or describe what the team chose (papers often state their choices before explaining them): leave all of that out. Do not list candidate options, do not mention methods or elements the team adopted as part of this decision, and do not say anything learned after it.
- "question": one short open question naming the decision, answerable in several different ways, e.g. "How should the team test whether the effect depends on the clean data?" It must not suggest an answer.
- "skip": true if the decision cannot be posed without stating its outcome, or is not a real choice (pure description). Otherwise false.
No names of people, labs, organisations, papers, models or datasets; no coined name for the phenomenon (describe it in plain words). Numbers are fine.

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "skip": bool, "context": str, "question": str}]}

ITEMS:

This is a revision. Each item also shows your previous context and question. Readers who knew what the team decided found that this version steers toward one particular resolution: it states or implies it, mentions elements that only one resolution would use, or frames the question so that one resolution is the obvious answer. You are still not told the decision. Rewrite the context and question so that several genuinely different resolutions answer the question equally directly: keep the facts any option needs, present facts that cut different ways neutrally, drop details that only matter to one particular resolution, and invent nothing.

=== key 6cd25fe52516
Kind of decision: how strongly to state a claim
Problem: How strongly to claim LIB's applicability overall
Write-up text before the decision: nd are very sparse in both PCA and LIB basis. ## 4 Conclusion We developed a novel interpretability method based on a transformation to the local interaction basis (LIB) and integrated gradient interaction graphs. Our work is built on the theoretical work by Bushnaq et al. (2024a) who propose representations based on parameterization-invariant structures in neural networks. LIB assumes that features in a neural network can be represented in a non-overcomplete basis. Additionally we assume that the main sources of freedom in the loss-landscape are linear dependencies in the activations of individual layers, and linear dependencies in the gradients between adjacent layers. LIB attempts to find a basis of sparsely interacting features for the activations of a neural network, represent the interactions between features in a graph, and identify modularity in the network’s computations by searching for modules in this graph. We find that our method produces more interpretable and more sparsely-interacting representations on toy models (a modular addition transformer and a CIFAR-10 model), compared to a baseline of using PCA directions as features. On language models, we find that LIB produces more sparsely-interacting representations than PCA in some layers, but the representations are not more interpretable. Furthermore, we do not find evidence of modularity in the interaction graphs produced by LIB on language models. Our goal was to test whether LIB could find a basis of features that would be more interpretable and interact much more sparsely than baseline methods (PCA).
Previous context: A research team developed an interpretability method that transforms network activations into a basis of sparsely interacting features and writes their conclusion. On toy models the method produced more interpretable and more sparsely interacting representations than a PCA baseline; on language models it was sparser in some layers but not more interpretable, and its interaction graphs showed no evidence of modularity.

=== key 37d2020504e2

Problem: At what level of abstraction/assumption to pursue alignment research
Write-up text before the decision: t insights for alignment coming from understanding DL's functionality and training process better. In general, different approaches to alignment make assumptions of different specificity and I roughly think of them in the following hierarchy (I’m omitting many approaches/ideas, just want to pump the intuition) * Agent foundations and other MIRI-type work: assumes that the AI system has goals and acts rationally. * Selection theorems and other John Wentworth-type work: the AI system is selected according to some fundamental selection principles. * ELK and heuristic arguments: assumes that the AI system has some internal model that we can interpret if the model is trained correctly and/or we have the right tools. * Science of DL: assumes that the AI system is a NN or a combination of NNs and has been trained with SGD or one of its many variants. * RLHF: assumes that the system is DL-based and can be fine-tuned to show good behavior by training it with human feedback. * Transformer mechanistic interpretability: Assumes that the relevant models are transformers and that a mechanistic understanding of the model is the key to aligning them. Obviously, I don’t claim that everyone who works on mechanistic interpretability for transformers thinks that this is the only necessary component of alignment. I’m just trying to put Science of DL into the context of the assumptions other approaches make. I personally believe that the Deep Learning paradigm is here to stay for at least another decade and is powerful enough to produce highly capable and potentially dangerous AI systems.

Reasons against Science of DL ============================= There are multiple good reasons to be skeptical of Science of DL as an alignment agenda and I definitely don’t think everyone should work on it. These include: 1. **Other agendas might be more promising:** There are a lot of alignment agendas out there. Most of them seem like they could solve some important subcomponent of alignment. I really wouldn’t want everyone to work on Science of DL and it’s good to take multiple bets and diversify as a community. 2. **The main problem doesn’t come from NNs:** Especially if you think that the core of the alignment problem comes from something that is not really related to NNs or how they are trained, e.g. if you believe the core of the alignment problem is agency or reward specification, Science of DL just seems like the wrong approach. 3. **It’s not neglected enough:** There are already people in academia and industry working on many of the questions related to Science of DL. It’s not clear that the AI safety community or EAs should use their time to work on it. 4. **Progress is too slow:** Questions around interpretability and generalization properties of NNs have been around for a long time. Most people would have hoped for much faster progress but we still can’t answer many basic questions about why NNs generalize and what concepts they learn. Final words ===========
